title: Where user-visible text hides in a web project: build configs, CI, store listings

census.why: A build config, read as code. The manifest inside it exists only at build time.
Head metadata is the surface most likely to be forgotten because it is not on screen.
An extension no JSON-driven scanner registers by default.
Shares a filename with the web manifest and means something else entirely.
Markdown nested inside YAML. Ordinary YAML tooling reports one opaque scalar.
Comments in a stylesheet — the miss two separate human passes both made on the reference repository.

An inline <style> and an inline <script>, which the markup scanner cannot read as prose. It used to read PAST both and still count their bytes as claimed, so this file would have reported a claimRatio of 1.0 — the extractor asserting it accounted for every byte — while three French strings inside them reached no site and no sweep. A false claim of full coverage is the one failure the whole accountability argument rests on not making.

expectations.find: 'Un atelier de publication pour petites équipes'
expectations.why: The manifest exists only at build time, so `find -name manifest.json` returns nothing and a filename-driven search misses the entire install listing. Found by STRUCTURE — `…/manifest/description` — not by the file's name.

Deliberately rspack rather than vite, so the rule is exercised on a bundler the reference repository never used. Anchored on `short_name` because `name: 'Atelier'` also matches it — which the runner reported rather than silently picking one.
A companion of the same rule. Translating a start_url breaks the installed app's entry point.
`.webmanifest` is an extension most scanners do not register as JSON.
Not translated and not left alone: RETARGETED. A manifest still declaring `fr` in an English build is a bug, and `locale-marker` is the only verdict that says so.
A store listing. The same filename as the web manifest, discriminated by `manifest_version` being present at all.
A match pattern looks like a URL because it is one. Translating it silently disables the extension.
A message bundle with its own schema: `/*/message` and `/*/description` are copy, `placeholders` are not.
Public-facing, and invisible to anyone grepping the application source.
A field id the template's own validation references. Two lines from a label that must move.

expectations.find: Pour tout ce qui n'est pas une anomalie
expectations.why: `config.yml` is covered by the same rule and lives beside the templates, so a case exercising only `bug.yml` would leave half of it untested.
Markdown nested inside YAML that renders on the public Releases page. Ordinary YAML tooling reports one opaque scalar and this line is invisible.
Shown in the Actions UI. A separate rule from the release body, in the same file.
An action reference. It sits in the same step as the release body that must be translated.

expectations.find: Un atelier de publication pour petites équipes.
expectations.why: Rendered by search engines and never on screen, which is why a visual review misses it.
The social preview. Same element, same attribute, different property.
Identical markup to the description beside it, and entirely machine-facing. Only the `name` attribute separates them.
The accessible name of an image. Copy by any definition, and easy to skip because it is an attribute.

expectations.find: Les commentaires d'une feuille de style sont de la prose
expectations.why: Four French comments in a stylesheet were what two separate human translation passes both missed on the reference repository.
Rendered on npmjs.com and by `npm search`, and read by everyone as dependency config.

expectations.find: Le style de la bannière, écrit à la main
expectations.why: A stylesheet HAS a reader, so the markup scanner now hands it the range instead of skipping it. Comments in a hand-written stylesheet are exactly where a whole-repo translation pass leaves residue.
A `content:` value renders on screen. Found for the same reason, and through the same extractor that reads a standalone .css.

There is no JavaScript reader here — the AST tier is async and belongs to `scan`, not to a markup scanner. So the bytes are declared UNREAD and the sweep covers them: the string is LISTED and G2 refuses, rather than being silently absent from a file claiming to be fully read. Listed, not claimed.

knownGaps: `html.title` cannot fire. The rule matches `{kind: attr, element: title, attr: text}`, but the HTML extractor emits a document title as a `prose-run` at `title/text[0]`. The title IS found and IS translated — by the generic prose path, with no rule cited — so the miss is in traceability rather than in recall.

`manifest/lang` inside `rspack.config.ts` comes back with no verdict at all, where the same field in `manifest.webmanifest` is a `locale-marker`. The companion matcher lists vite, nuxt, astro and next; its parent rule lists nine more bundlers including rspack. A locale marker left undetected in a build config is exactly the G6 `locale-drift` finding this tool advertises.

An inline <script> is swept rather than parsed, so its strings arrive as `unclassified` instead of carrying container semantics. Routing the body to the AST tier would give real verdicts; it needs the async grammar load that lives in `scan`, and the sweep already makes the text impossible to miss.
